scenario: AITA for my gf and I keeping our income low to apply for lower income housing. | Ok so this is weird. My girlfriend and I have been looking to move in together so we’ve been searching for apartments. My parents recently onformed me that they’d be moving to Phoenix, AZ in August so I would need to find my own place. A lot of the apartments were too expensive for our budget but we found 1 that we’re happy with. The complex was very nice and the lost cost we were told was 890/mo for 1 bed/1 bath. We were also informed of this application where if you and whoever are living in the apartment are making less than 32000 collectively a year then you apply for the “bond program” (I think it was called) that let’s you live in their studio apartments for less rent (about 550 a month not including utilities) We asked about the availability of the apartment and they told us that there are a lot available right now so it’s not like people are scrambling to get in. My gf has been looking for a new job and would like to switch to full time when she finishes college. I told her that she should wait until we apply and get the verification that we apply for the program to actually go full time and she agreed. We wouldn’t apply until July. (She’s not struggling for cash or anything and i would help out if that ever were the case, this would strictly be to save money in the long run). We also started trying to attack our debts together and would be basically living like poor people for the foreseeable future until we were out of debt. So this program would give us a head start. After the leasing period, if your income rises above 32000 a year you’d be asked to move into the normal studio (which is the same size and specs as the bond program one). We cooould afford to live in the normal apartments comfortably but it would take longer to pay off our debts. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out if it's morally acceptable for me and my girlfriend to keep our income low so we can apply for lower-income housing. Let me break this down step by step.

First, we're planning to move in together, and we found an apartment that's a bit expensive for our current budget. But there's this bond program where if our combined income is below $32,000 a year, we can get a cheaper rent. That sounds great because it would help us save money, especially since we're trying to pay off our debts.

My girlfriend is about to finish college and wants to switch to a full-time job. I suggested she wait until after we apply for the bond program in July. She agreed, so she's not going to take a full-time job right away. We're not struggling financially, and I can help out if needed, but the main goal is to save money and pay off our debts faster.

The complex has a lot of available apartments, so it's not like we're in a rush to get in. After the lease period, if our income goes above $32,000, we'd have to move into the normal studio apartment, which we can afford but would take longer to pay off our debts. We think this program would give us a head start.

Now, is this morally acceptable? I'm not sure. On one hand, we're trying to save money and manage our debts responsibly. On the other hand, we're keeping our income low to qualify for a lower rent, which might be seen as manipulating the system.

I wonder if the bond program is intended for people who genuinely can't afford higher rent. If we're doing this just to save money, even though we can afford the normal rent, is that fair? It might be taking a spot away from someone who really needs it.

But then again, we're not lying about our income or anything. We're just choosing not to increase our income right now to qualify for the lower rent. Is that different from lying? I'm not sure.

Also, the complex has plenty of available apartments, so maybe it's not affecting others as much. If there were a shortage, it might be more of an issue, but since there are many available, maybe it's not as bad.

I'm also thinking about the long-term benefits. By saving money now, we can pay off our debts faster and be in a better financial position overall. That seems responsible.

But I'm still concerned about whether it's fair to use the program when we could afford the normal rent. It feels like we're taking advantage of a system meant for people with lower incomes. Even though we're not lying, the intent is to save money, not because we can't afford it.

Maybe there's a middle ground. If the program allows people to stay in the lower rent even if their income increases, as long as they meet the criteria at the time of application, then it's okay. But if the intention is for ongoing low-income support, then maybe it's not.

I'm also considering the rules of the bond program. If it's designed for people who are currently low-income, then our plan might be against the spirit of the program, even if we're not breaking any rules.

In the end, I'm torn between being responsible with our finances and potentially taking advantage of a program meant for others. I need to decide if this action is morally acceptable or not.
